This report is to present the transportation functional design that has been developed to address safety and operational issues for eastbound traffic on 22nd Street West between defen Baker Drive and Confederation Drive. Next slide, please. Thanks. Safety and operational issues exist on 22nd Street West between defen Baker Drive and Confederation Drive in the eastbound direction. This location has long standing
concerns with the operation of vehicles attempting to maneuver from Fairmont Drive across three lanes of traffic to turn left from 22nd Street eastbound to Confederation Drive northbound.
Several measures have been installed over the years in an attempt to prevent this movement. These include concrete barriers, low profile barriers, and tough curves with delineator posts.

As you can see from some of the images, they have had very little success. Each of the measures have been removed. Based on the available collision records for the intersection, there have been no fatal or severe injury collisions in the past five years.
41 minor injury collisions and 142 collisions resulting in property damage only.

In terms of vulnerable road users, there were two minor injury collisions involving pedestrians, one minor injury collision with a cyclist and one collision with a cyclist which resulted in property damage only.
Eastbound traffic made up 37% of the total number of collisions at the intersection, while only accounting for 25% of the traffic volumes.
So this indicates an overrepresentation for this direction of travel in the collision data. Next slide please.
The Circle Drive West functional planning study recommended geometric changes for this intersection to address these ongoing traffic safety and operational issues.
And identified an eastbound slotted left turn line as a short term improvement that could be implemented prior to the construction of the recommended Circle Drive and 22nd Street West interchange.

This report provides an overview of a pilot project involving the retrofit of two city of Saskatoon heavy duty trucks
with enhanced visibility and collision prediction systems and the evaluation of their effectiveness.
The city's heavy duty trucks and equipment are not currently equipped with pedestrian or cyclist proximity detection systems.
The city has partnered with a local vendor and initiated a proof of concept pilot project to assess two different types of systems as potential options for enhanced visibility for heavy duty trucks.
The administration has selected a waste collection and an asphalt patching track for the pilot project.
These trucks often work in areas with pedestrians and cyclists at present.

The pilot project includes the installation of a 360 degree camera system and a collision prediction system in the waste collection track and the installation of a 360 degree artificial intelligence enhanced camera system in the asphalt patching track.
The purpose of the pilot project is to assess the effectiveness of these systems in providing enhanced visibility and warning the driver of blind spot hazards.
The systems are being piloted from mid June to mid September 2024.
This trail period may be extended to collect additional information such as how the equipment works in cold weather and in winter driving conditions.
Once the trail period is completed, the driver feedback will be used to assess the effectiveness of the piloted systems.

In addition, the administration has reached out to transport Canada and is planning to meet with them to learn more about any research underway regarding enhanced visibility for heavy duty trucks.
Information gathered through the pilot project will be used to guide the next steps and decisions.
